python.Rule Sub-heading: "break" and "continue" should not be used outside a loop
python.Rule-Details: break and continue are unstructured control flow statements which make code harder to read. Additionally, more recent versions of Python raise a SyntaxError when modules containing break or continue outside of a loop are imported. Therefore, these statements should not be used outside of loops.

python.Rule Sub-heading: "Exception" and "BaseException" should not be raised
python.Rule-Details: Raising instances of Exception and BaseException will have a negative impact on any code trying to catch these exceptions. It is recommended to raise more specific exceptions or create custom exception classes.

python.Rule Sub-heading: "pass" should not be used needlessly
python.Rule-Details: The use of a pass statement where it's not required by the syntax is pure cruft and should be removed.

python.Rule Sub-heading: A field should not duplicate the name of its containing class
python.Rule-Details: Best practice dictates that any field or member with the same name as the enclosing class be renamed to be more descriptive.

python.Rule Sub-heading: All "except" blocks should be able to catch exceptions
python.Rule-Details: In some contexts an except block is dead code as it will never catch any exception. The order of exception handlers should be considered carefully to ensure proper exception handling.

python.Rule Sub-heading: All code should be reachable
python.Rule-Details: Jump statements like return, break, continue, and raise move control flow out of the current code block, leading to dead code.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Alternation in regular expressions should not contain empty alternatives
python.Rule-Details: If one of the alternatives in a regex is empty, it would match any input, which is most probably a mistake.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Boolean checks should not be inverted
python.Rule-Details: It is needlessly complex to invert the result of a boolean comparison.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Break, continue and return statements should not occur in "finally" blocks
python.Rule-Details: Using return, break or continue in a finally block suppresses the propagation of any unhandled exception.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Character classes should be preferred over reluctant quantifiers in regular expressions
python.Rule-Details: Reluctant quantifiers can lead to inefficient regex performance. It's better to use character classes when possible.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Collapsible "if" statements should be merged
python.Rule-Details: Merging collapsible if statements increases the code's readability.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Comments should not be located at the end of lines of code
python.Rule-Details: Single-line comments should be placed on their own line preceding the code they describe.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Conditional expressions should not be nested
python.Rule-Details: Nesting conditional expressions makes code harder to read; clarity should be prioritized using separate statements.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Control flow statements "if", "for", "while", "try" and "with" should not be nested too deeply
python.Rule-Details: Nested control flow statements can make code hard to read. The maximum allowed depth is 4.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Docstrings should be defined
python.Rule-Details: Docstrings should document what the code does, its return values, and requirements. They should be enclosed in triple double-quotes.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Instance and class methods should have at least one positional parameter
python.Rule-Details: Instance methods should have a 'self' parameter. Class methods should have a 'cls' parameter.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Loops without "break" should not have "else" clauses
python.Rule-Details: A loop's else clause is skipped when break is executed. Without a break, else is effectively always executed and should be removed.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Methods and properties that don't access instance data should be static
python.Rule-Details: Methods not accessing instance data should be decorated with @staticmethod to improve performance.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Redundant pairs of parentheses should be removed
python.Rule-Details: Redundant parentheses can be misleading and should be removed for clarity.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Sections of code should not be commented out
python.Rule-Details: Commented-out code should be removed to improve readability; it can be retrieved from version control if needed.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Statements should be on separate lines
python.Rule-Details: For better readability, do not put more than one statement on a single line.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Unused function parameters should be removed
python.Rule-Details: Unused parameters are misleading and should be removed to clarify function behavior, unless needed for compatibility with other APIs.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Unused private nested classes should be removed
python.Rule-Details: Unused private nested classes are dead code that should be removed to prevent confusion and reduce code size.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Comparison to singleton
python.Rule-Details: Comparisons to None should use is or is not, rather than equality operators.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Prefix or suffix check
python.Rule-Details: Use `str.startswith()` and `str.endswith()` for checking prefixes and suffixes instead of string slicing.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Object type comparisons
python.Rule-Details: Always use isinstance() for object type comparisons.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Empty sequences
python.Rule-Details: For sequences, use the fact that empty sequences are false in boolean contexts.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Comparison of boolean statements
python.Rule-Details: Avoid comparing boolean values to True or False using ==, instead rely on the boolean context.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Bare except clauses should not be used
python.Rule-Details: Using a bare except: clause catches all exceptions including SystemExit and KeyboardInterrupt, making it hard to interrupt a program. Always specify the exception type(s) to catch. Use except Exception: if you need to catch all standard exceptions.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Mutable default arguments should not be used
python.Rule-Details: Default argument values are evaluated once at function definition time, not each time the function is called. Mutable defaults (list, dict, set) are shared across all calls and can lead to unexpected behavior. Use None as default and initialize inside the function.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Wildcard imports should not be used
python.Rule-Details: Avoid using 'from module import *' as it pollutes the namespace, makes it unclear where names come from, and can cause name conflicts. Import specific names or use qualified imports.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Avoid lambda assignments
python.Rule-Details: Assigning a lambda to a variable defeats the purpose of lambda (anonymous functions). Use 'def' to define named functions instead. This improves stack traces and readability.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Use join() for string concatenation in loops
python.Rule-Details: String concatenation using += in loops is inefficient due to string immutability. Use ''.join() or list comprehension with join for better performance.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Use context managers for resource handling
python.Rule-Details: Files and other resources should be managed using 'with' statements (context managers) to ensure proper cleanup even if exceptions occur. Avoid manual open/close patterns.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Imports should be organized and grouped
python.Rule-Details: Imports should be grouped in the following order: standard library, third-party packages, local application imports. Within each group, imports should be alphabetically sorted. Groups should be separated by blank lines.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Avoid using eval() and exec()
python.Rule-Details: eval() and exec() execute arbitrary code and pose serious security risks. They should be avoided unless absolutely necessary and input is fully sanitized. Consider safer alternatives like ast.literal_eval() for parsing.

python.Rule Sub-heading: Python example structure
python.Rule-Details: Python examples should call sys.exit(1) on failure and use an if __name__ == "__main__": guard that invokes the example from a separate function.

cpp.Rule-Details: goto statements must not be used.
nullptr must be used instead of 0 or NULL when assigning or comparing null pointer values.
Constants (constexpr, const) or enumerations should be used instead of #define.
All callback functions must be suffixed with a '_cb'.
Use 'using' for type aliases instead of 'typedef' for better readability and consistency with modern C++. Example: using size_type_t = size_t; using callback_func_t = void(*)(int);
Each source statement must assign a value to no more than one variable. Multiple variable assignments, such as 'a = b = c;' must not be used.

Structures should be initialized completely, either using aggregate initialization or alternative methods. Example: struct SomeStruct {int x; int y; SomeStruct *pNext;}; SomeStruct someData{}; 
SomeStruct moreData{.x=9, .y=0, .pNext = &someData};

Any time a case statement is used without a corresponding break by design, the [[fallthrough]] attribute must be used. Example: switch (operation) {case OpGo: break; case OpStop: [[fallthrough]]; default: break;}
When testing non-booleans, if (x != 0) or if (x != nullptr) must be used instead of if (x).
Subexpressions in if statements that use comparison operators must have explicit bracketing. Example: if ((pResource == nullptr) && (flags.abort == true) && (id >= MinIdToCheck)) {...}
Yoda conditions such as if (nullptr != x) should not be used.
When expecting a result of a wider type, convert the integer type to a larger size.
Magic numbers must not be used. Use enumerations or constants to convey the significance of the value.
Use binary literals and digit separators wherever it helps readability.
Methods must be declared const when they do not modify object state.
Input parameters passed by reference must be const unless mutation is required by the API contract.
A loop must not contain more than one loop variable.
The loop variable should be declared within the loop declaration and not used outside the loop.
A loop must not contain more than one termination condition in the loop header. Multiple if-break statements within the loop body are acceptable.
The contents of a for loop must not alter the value of the loop variable.
Use range based loops where suitable, such as iterating through arrays.
A local variable must be declared in the innermost scope possible.
Perform a null check before dereferencing a pointer if there is a possibility for it to be null.
Use call by reference in favor of calls using pointer arguments.
Do not return a pointer or reference to a local object.
Remove unused parameters from functions and methods, unless required by interface compliance, callback signatures, virtual method overrides, or API compatibility.
Objects should be initialized when created. Check member variable initialization in constructors.
Methods must not be implemented in header files, except inline functions and template definitions.
Initialize non-static member variables during construction, preferably in the header file.
Use one of the following prefixes for naming Boolean variables or methods: 'is', 'should', 'has', 'can'.
Do not use auto, unless for iterators, range-based loops, or complex template types where it improves readability.

Prefer static_cast over functional cast or C-style cast. Use static_cast for explicit type conversions when possible. Preferred int x = static_cast<int>(3.14); Acceptable int y = int(3.14); Avoid int z = (int)3.14; Use dynamic_cast for polymorphic types, const_cast for const removal, and reinterpret_cast for low-level casts only when necessary.

Within a function or code block, maintain consistency in casting style. If one casting style has been used, continue using the same style throughout that block. Consistent - all static_cast void process() { int x = static_cast<int>(value1); int y = static_cast<int>(value2);} Inconsistent - mixing styles. void process() { int x = static_cast<int>(value1); int y = (int)value2;  // Avoid mixing
}
All array-type objects, including vectors, that are allocated or resized must be ringfenced with try-catch and return da_status_memory_error on allocation failure.
All instances allocated with new must be deleted. All arrays allocated with new[] must be properly delete[]d.
APIs that return da_status must return da_status_success on successful completion. Do not use a literal 0 in place of da_status_success.
Examples and test executables that return a process exit code must return 0 on successful completion and a non-zero value otherwise to remain compatible with CTest.

For all public APIs that have a handle (i.e., handle or store), they must call handle->clear() immediately after the handle null check, before any other validation or processing, to reset any previous error state.

Examples must be well-structured with clear comments explaining each step, demonstrate a realistic use case without unnecessary complexity, and follow a consistent pattern that users can adapt as a template. Avoid overly trivial examples (e.g., single API call with no context) and overly complex ones (e.g., multiple unrelated features in one example).
Examples must avoid numerical issues such as near-zero division, poor matrix conditioning, or use of extreme values in example data.
Given the example input data, the output must be uniquely defined.

Examples must check the returned status of every relevant API call and gracefully handle the condition. On non-successful status return, identify if the API still returns relevant results (e.g., iterative methods stopping with sub-optimal solutions).
When printing a numerical result, examples must also print a message indicating whether the result is within the expected tolerance, where appropriate.
Public C++ API functions must have corresponding C overloads in aoclda_c_wrapper.cpp.
Public C++ API functions must have corresponding Python bindings.

Public API documentation (Doxygen comments) must include: (1) a high-level description of the implemented algorithm, including maximum expected error or tolerance where applicable; (2) all inputs and outputs sufficiently explained and marked as [in]/[out]; (3) all returned errors listed and explained, with advice on how to rectify where available; (4) references or links to example sources where they exist.

Variable and function names must be short, descriptive, and consistent with those of similar functions in the codebase. Names should clearly convey purpose without being overly abbreviated or unnecessarily long. Avoid single-character names except for loop indices (i, j, k) and well-known mathematical conventions (n, m, x, y). Avoid generic names like data, info, temp, val, or result when a more specific name is possible. When a name is unclear or inconsistent with similar code, suggest a better alternative.
